summary: This document describes how to carry multicast trees created by PIM-SM in Any-Source Multicast mode over Multipoint LDP (mLDP) point-to-multipoint paths when they cross an MPLS domain.

eli5.summary: When a group broadcast has to cross a provider's network, it needs a path. This note shows how to turn the multicast tree into a matching path there.

subtitle: Two ways to carry PIM-SM any-source multicast trees across an MPLS core using mLDP point-to-multipoint paths.

tldr.problem: Multicast trees built by PIM-SM in Any-Source Multicast (ASM) mode sometimes have to cross an MPLS domain, and RFC 6826 only covered source-specific (SSM) trees.
tldr.mechanism: Each IP multicast tree is mapped one-to-one to a point-to-multipoint LSP signalled by mLDP. Mechanism 1 maps only source trees, with BGP Source Active auto-discovery routes. Mechanism 2 also carries shared trees, using two new TLVs.
tldr.outcome: Mechanism 2 is REQUIRED for conforming implementations and Mechanism 1 is OPTIONAL. A network deploys one or the other, not both.

today: RFC 7442 is a Proposed Standard published in February 2015. The unit metadata shows no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Introduction and Scope
sections.content:
RFC 6826 describes how to map Point-to-Multipoint Label Switched Paths (P2MP LSPs) created by mLDP to multicast trees created by PIM-SM in Source-Specific Multicast (SSM) mode. RFC 7442 does the same for PIM-SM in Any-Source Multicast (ASM) mode, and describes two possible mechanisms.

The first mechanism is OPTIONAL for implementations. The second is REQUIRED for all implementations claiming conformance. From a deployment point of view they are mutually exclusive: one network can deploy either one, but not both.

Like RFC 6826, each IP multicast tree is mapped one-to-one to a P2MP LSP. The RFC says this works well when the number of LSPs is under the control of the MPLS operator, or is known to be limited. The existing BGP Multicast VPN procedures of RFC 6514 can also map Internet multicast trees to P2MP LSPs, including aggregation of several trees onto one LSP, but their details are out of scope here.
sections.eli5: There are two ways to do the job, like two different roads to the same town. A network picks one road and sticks with it.

sections.title: When Source Active Routes Are Needed
sections.content:
Suppose the provider has set up the network so the Rendezvous Point (RP) for an ASM group G is always between the receivers and the sources. Then the ingress Provider Edge (PE) for (S,G) is always the same as the ingress PE for the RP, and the Source Active auto-discovery routes are never needed. If the network is known to be provisioned this way, mLDP in-band signaling can use the different procedures in RFC 7438.

A service provider provisions its PE routers to use either the procedures of RFC 7438 or those of this document. The reader is expected to know PIM-SM (RFC 4601) and mLDP (RFC 6388). The document also assumes a given Label Switching Router (LSR) may have some IP multicast capable interfaces and other MPLS capable interfaces.
sections.eli5: If the meeting spot is always on the way, nobody needs extra messages telling where the speakers are. When it is not, the extra messages are needed.

sections.title: Mechanism 1: Shared Trees Stay Outside
sections.content:
This mechanism does not carry IP multicast shared trees over the MPLS network. When an LSR creates (*,G) state from PIM messages on an IP multicast interface, it does not propagate that state in mLDP.

Instead, whenever an RP learns of a new multicast source (through PIM Register or MSDP messages), the RP SHOULD originate a BGP Source Active auto-discovery route. It carries one MCAST-VPN NLRI with the Route Distinguisher set to 0, the Multicast Source field set to S and the Multicast Group field set to G, each with its length field set for IPv4 or IPv6. The route SHOULD carry the NO_EXPORT Community (RFC 1997) to keep it inside the advertising Autonomous System. When the source is no longer active, the RP MUST withdraw the route.

An LSR that has a (*,G) entry with a non-empty outgoing interface list containing IP multicast interfaces MUST check for Source Active routes for that G. If a route exists, S is reachable via an MPLS interface, and the LSR has no (S,G) state, it originates an mLDP Label Map with the Transit IPv4/IPv6 Source TLV carrying (S,G), as in RFC 6826. An LSR that receives a new Source Active route does the same check against its existing (*,G) entries. Creating or deleting (S,G,RPT-bit) state triggers no mLDP or BGP action.
sections.eli5: The rendezvous point shouts out which speakers are active. Routers that have listeners for that group then build a private path straight to each speaker.

sections.title: Mechanism 2: Shared Tree TLVs
sections.content:
This mechanism lets shared trees cross the MPLS network. When an LSR creates (*,G) state from PIM messages on an IP multicast interface, it propagates that state in mLDP. To do so, the document defines two new mLDP TLVs: the Transit IPv4 Shared Tree TLV and the Transit IPv6 Shared Tree TLV.

They are encoded exactly like the IPv4/IPv6 Source Tree TLVs of RFC 6826, except that an RP field carrying the address of the RP replaces the Source field. In the IPv4 TLV, Type is 11, Length is 8, and RP and Group are 4 octets each. In the IPv6 TLV, Type is 12, Length is 32, and RP and Group are 16 octets each.

The in-band signaling procedures are the same as for source trees in RFC 6826, except that (*,G) state is signalled with the Shared Tree TLVs instead of (S,G) state with the Source TLVs.
sections.eli5: The new labels say which meeting spot and which group a path is for. They work like the old labels, which named a speaker instead of a meeting spot.

sections.title: Source Active Routes and Pruning in Mechanism 2
sections.content:
An LSR that creates (S,G) state from an mLDP Label Map with the Transit Source TLV MUST originate a Source Active route if all of these are true: S is reachable via an IP-multicast-capable interface, G is in the PIM-SM ASM range, and the LSR has no (*,G) state with an IP-multicast-capable interface as incoming interface. The route is built as in Mechanism 1, carries NO_EXPORT, and MUST be withdrawn when the (S,G) state is deleted. No route is originated if the LSR already has (*,G) state learned through a Shared Tree TLV with the RP reachable over an IP multicast interface. Receiving Source Active routes works the same as in Mechanism 1.

For pruning sources off the shared tree, the LSR MUST move the (S,G,RPT-bit) downstream state to Prune when it has a (*,G) entry whose incoming interface list contains an IP interface, whose outgoing list contains an MPLS interface, and it does not originate an mLDP Label Map for (S,G) with the Source TLV. Conceptually this acts as if it had received Prune(S,G,rpt) on an MPLS interface. The LSR MUST keep that state in Prune while the (*,G) outgoing list contains an MPLS interface, at least one Source Active route for (S,G) exists, and it does not originate the (S,G) Label Map. When any of these stops being true, it MUST return to NoInfo.
sections.eli5: If a router is already getting a speaker's message another way, it tells the shared path to stop repeating it. When that stops being true, the router goes back to listening normally.

sections.title: IANA and Security Considerations
sections.content:
IANA maintains the registry "Label Distribution Protocol (LDP) Parameters" with a subregistry "LDP MP Opaque Value Element basic type". It has allocated value 11 to the Transit IPv4 Shared Tree TLV and 12 to the Transit IPv6 Shared Tree TLV.

All the security considerations for mLDP (RFC 6388) apply. From a security point of view, using Shared Tree TLVs is no different from using Source TLVs (RFC 6826).
sections.eli5: The new labels get official numbers in a public list. They are no riskier than the old labels, so the same safety rules apply.

items.label: Transit IPv4 Shared Tree TLV
items.desc: Length 8: a 4-octet RP address and a 4-octet group address.

items.label: Transit IPv6 Shared Tree TLV
items.desc: Length 32: a 16-octet RP address and a 16-octet group address.
